translations.text: Brilliant and altogether beautiful are the words of the holy Scriptures, which were written by the grace of the Holy Spirit to instruct all believers and to adorn the holy Church.
By them she is adorned like a bride clothed in glory, and she adorns her children with the radiance of her beauty.

And as with the flowers of the field, she makes fragrant the gathering of those who love learning, and stirs them to follow by scent the trail of her ointments and to pursue the fragrance of her incense.
For once she was joined to that Bridegroom of purified souls, from then on she brought after her the gatherings of the faithful,
who were called her companions because of the beauty of their spiritual adornment and the varied loveliness of their many kinds of virtue, as though adorned with fringes embroidered in gold,
And since the queen stood at the king's right hand in the royal palaces, and so that these too might be made worthy to stand with her in the great assembly of the firstborn, as David says:
"In the great church I will confess you," where God among gods was made known through them,
whom he foreknew and also predestined to receive that honor of deification. Among them was counted this great and brilliant,
altogether desirable and beloved father of ours, Hilarion, lofty in his struggle for the virtues and loftier still in his ascent from strength to strength in the power of spiritual contemplation.
Our discourse is about him, and our task is to write down his life and conduct and recount it to later generations,
like a golden monument adorned with precious stones and pearls of great price, raised up and standing in the midst of the church,
so that those who enter the stadium of ascetic struggle may look upon it and be stirred more ardently to imitate and resemble his brilliance.
Although he was recent in time, yet among those ancient and most eminent ascetics,

he equaled some in virtue and in the working of miracles, he surpassed others, and with some he even went forth [?] side by side, through his love of exile even unto death and his complete self-effacement.
But let us not prolong our discourse, since we have not taken the path of encomium.
Rather, we are eager to write down his life, to fill the ears of those who love to listen with spiritual sweetness, and to recount
where this saint sprang from, and from what regions this new and all-brilliant luminary arose,
who rose in the east and with the lightning of his virtues illumined those who dwell in the west.
This blessed and holy father of ours, Hilarion, was Georgian by race.

Many saints and wonder-working men have come from that people. Although they have been forgotten over the many years because their lives were not written down, they nevertheless stand in brilliance before God.

However, for some recently manifested saints, both their memory has survived and their life has been written down by God-loving and zealous men, as with this saint, who is the subject of our discourse.
But let us come to the first course of our discourse and tell you every aspect of his life, as we said before.
This blessed man came from the land of Kartli, from the borders of the region of Kakheti. He was the child of rich and distinguished nobles (aznaurs).
His father had other children as well, but this holy one had been vowed to God by his parents, as Samuel was long ago by Hannah.
When he was six years old, he was given to be taught by a worthy and God-loving man who lived in his village,
where the blessed one's father lived, and this man taught him the spiritual books day and night.
He was watered like a tree planted by God beside the streams of the waters of the Holy Spirit, which are the God-inspired books.
When his father saw how eagerly the boy was learning from that holy elder, he began to give generously everything that was needed, and he set about building up that place into a monastery.
Brothers gathered there, only about sixteen in number. His father kept coming, both to build up the place and to see his beloved son.
When the blessed one, the true son of the heavenly Father, saw his father's repeated visits,
he was grieved by this, and he remembered the words of the holy Gospel:
"Whoever does not leave his father and his mother, and does not take up his cross and follow me, is not worthy of me." So he resolved to go away into the inner desert.
He got up and went to the desert of Gareja. There he found many ascetic men, and near them a small cave.
He rejoiced with great joy, went in, and settled there.
He was about fifteen years old. From then on he began to enter the racecourse of ascetic struggle.
With fasting and vigils he wore down his youthful age. By prayer and constant contemplation of God he became like the bodiless beings,
until he surpassed in ascetic struggle all who lived in that place in the desert, for everyone marveled at how great his labor and endurance were.
All the brothers were edified by his teaching, and they fell at his feet asking to be allowed to live with him.
He accepted about eleven brothers to live with him, ascetics who were meek and humble.
They were like angels in their fasting and in their unceasing prayer and hymns to God, until the report of his holiness spread through the whole land of Kartli,
for how could a lamp be hidden under a bushel or under a bed and not be made known to everyone?
In time the bishop of Ruisi also learned of the abundance of his virtues. He was filled with spiritual longing, and he got up and went to visit him.
When he reached the holy man, they greeted each other with a holy kiss.
When the bishop saw his pale face, his humble speech and his poor clothing, he was amazed with a thoughtful amazement and said to him:
"For a long time I have wanted to see you, my son Hilarion. I, a sinner, have been found worthy to receive your holy prayer.
For this I thank God all the more, for He has not left me deprived of your spiritual love.
And now I beg you, my son, to fulfill my wish and receive the priesthood from me, poor and unworthy as I am."
But the blessed one, since he was entirely humble and a stranger to human glory,
He did not wish to rise to the honour of the priesthood. He resisted that worthy bishop, begged him earnestly and refused, asking to be set free from the yoke of the priesthood.
But the bishop, moved by God, pressed him again and pleaded with him. When the saint saw that he was being compelled,
he judged that disobeying the high priest would be a sin. Given courage by God through power from above, he said to him:
"O honourable father, I, this poor man, am in your hands. Whatever your worthiness wishes, let it be done to me."
Then the holy bishop rose and ordained him a priest. They celebrated the holy mystery and received communion together.
The bishop went away and told all the people about his virtues, and those who heard it gave thanks to God.
Many people came from distant lands to see him and to receive his holy prayer.
After this, when blessed Hilarion saw the crowds of people coming to him, it grieved him and he began to be troubled.
While still in the years of his youth he gained the spirit of an old man, like the great Moses, and he became a judge between the soul and the body.
He took the side of the one that was despised and weakened. He killed the pride of the flesh and buried it in the sand of humility, where no fodder for the passions can grow.
Then, when he saw that the powers of darkness would not stop stirring up trouble in that Egypt of the passions, he left everything that belonged to Pharaoh with Pharaoh himself, the tyrant.
He withdrew and climbed the mountain of the virtues. There he shepherded good thoughts like sheep on the green pasture of ascetic struggle.

By contemplating these visible things he was lifted up to an understanding of the invisible. There he saw the living bush of the spirit blazing within the passion of his own flesh, burning him without consuming him.
But let us return to our earlier account. The saint was seized by a desire to live as a stranger in a foreign land, and by a hatred of vainglory.
More than this, and above all, he longed to venerate the holy and life-giving places
where the Word of God, who cannot suffer, took sufferings upon himself for our sake in this human flesh, which he took from us.
As he had planned, he chose one of the brethren, a brother who surpassed all the others in virtue and was able to lead as superior and to shepherd souls.
He appointed this brother as superior in his own place. Then he took one brother with him and set out for the holy city of Jerusalem. They travelled well, guided by God.
After they had travelled for many days, they reached the land of Sham (Syria), where barbarian peoples lived.
On their journey they met wicked robbers on the road. At once, like wild beasts, the robbers fell on them, as was the habit of their minds.
They drew their swords to strike them and raised them to strike holy Hilarion first. At once their hands withered, and they could not bring them down.
Then they began to weep and plead with him, and they followed after them for about five stadia.
When his merciful soul saw this, he remembered the commandment of the Saviour, which he speaks in the Gospel:
"Do not repay evil for evil." Then the saint turned back to them, made the sign of the cross, healed them, and sent them away alive.
And when they saw how quickly they had been healed, they brought him bread and carob pods,
and they asked forgiveness and spoke to him in their own language, in a way he could understand, promising that they would never again do such things to monks.
And one of them went with him until he reached the holy Mount Tabor, where Christ our God was transfigured in glory before his holy disciples.
They prayed there and venerated that holy mountain, and from there they went to the holy city of Jerusalem and made pilgrimage to the holy and venerable places, and
there the holy man saw every form of the dispensation of the Word of God, and he venerated holy and glorious Golgotha and the life-giving Tomb.
And from there he went to Bethlehem and saw the cave that imitates heaven, where our Lord Jesus Christ was born of the holy Virgin; he kissed it fervently and venerated it with longing.
And from there he reached the holy river Jordan and bathed in that holy water, and he visited all the monasteries that had been built in those holy deserts.
And he went as far as the Lavra of the great Sabas. And he spent seven years in all those deserts in ascetic struggles and labors that cannot be put into words.
For he had freed himself from all the material things and cares of the world and made himself ready to understand the Most High, as David says:
"Be still and know that I am God." And he settled within himself
and dwelt alone with the One alone, the Desired One. From then on, who could tell how many struggles and labors he took upon himself?
For in living as a stranger in exile, in poverty, and in his love of destitution he became equal to those who were perfect and renowned for ascetic struggle,

and in courage, in love of wisdom, in fighting bravely against the invisible enemies, and in mercilessly wearing down his own flesh, he became like all those who have humbled themselves and become strangers for God's sake.
By gathering both of these measures within himself, he was found equal to the perfect in both respects, and because of this he came to share closely in the continual vision of God.
For action is the beginning of contemplation, and godly, wise fear brings fearlessness, since the one who fears no longer fears like a slave,

nor is he zealous like a hired worker for the sake of wages. Rather, as a beloved and dear son of the Father, he has reached the third degree of perfection and gazes on the Desired One more highly than at first,
and from then on he is eager only to converse with Him without ever being parted from Him, just as this holy father of ours Hilarion was.
For while he was living this way in the deserts of the Jordan, as we said before, and especially in the great Lavra of Father Sabas,
all the fathers were amazed at his struggles and labors, which were beyond nature, and by everyone he was spoken of as something marvelous and pointed out with the finger, as the apostle says:
"We have been made a spectacle to the world, to angels and to men." And he always prayed to God to reveal to him what was best for his soul, whatever was pleasing to His mercy.
And he would say the words of the psalm: "Make known to me, O Lord, the way in which I should walk, and teach me also to do your will," and what follows.
And when he had spent seven years in such struggle, praying to God, one night,
when he had finished his appointed rule of prayer and, because of the heaviness of the body's nature, had fallen asleep for a little while, he saw a vision like this:
it was as though he was carried away to the holy Mount of Olives, from which our Lord Jesus Christ ascended in glory to heaven, to the Father, from where he had also come down.
And he saw the holy Queen, the Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, and twelve shining men standing before her.
And as he was gazing at this wondrous vision, the holy Queen said to him:
"O Hilarion, go and hurry to your home, and prepare a supper for the Lord, my Son."
And when he woke from the vision, he at once understood the meaning of what he had seen and of the divine command.
He rose and offered thanks to the good God and to his all-holy Mother for this most excellent revelation.
And he set out for his own country and to his own people, filled with courage from above, as Moses did long before,
that great lawgiver, who turned back to Egypt a second time to lead out his afflicted people.
In the same way this man also received the command to return to the very place where he was born and raised, so that he might help those of his own nature who were enslaved to the invisible Pharaoh.
So then, just as his first departure was good and wholly beautiful in God's sight, because of the immaturity of his spiritual age, his return to that same place was even better and more beautiful,
since he received the command there, clothed with power by hope from above, to help those oppressed by the enemy, in accordance with the saying of the wise man:
"There is a time for everything." And again Jeremiah says: "Whoever brings out the precious from the worthless shall be as my mouth."
For this reason the holy man came to his own country. And when he arrived, he found that his father and his brothers had died.
And he mourned them with natural grief. Then he rose, offered thanks to God, and prayed for their repose and blessedness.
His mother brought him all of his father's property and said to him: "Spend this, my son, as seems good to you."
The blessed Hilarion first of all took care of his mother's living, as was proper, for honouring one's parents is commanded in the law, both the Old and the New.
And he built a monastery for nuns in a good and beautiful place, brought his worthy mother into it, and cared for her with a son's devotion.
And he gave it a number of villages, as far as he was able.
And he laid down a rule and canon for them, as is proper for life in a monastery: for prayer, fasting and all orderly conduct.
And he became a father and spiritual teacher to his own mother according to the flesh.
He also built another monastery for monks and gathered into it about seventy-six brothers, worthy men who practised the ascetic struggle,
whose holiness and worth he saw with spiritual eyes. And he laid down a rule and canon for them too, suited to their strength.
He built a church for it and adorned it with every kind of ornament. He acquired holy books and placed them in it, and he gave it the villages that remained from his family estate.
When he had finished it and supplied everything it needed, he divided all the rest of the property from his estate among the poor and the helpless.
Having thus rightly freed himself of the wealth of his estate, he offered thanks to God, who brings all good things to completion.
But when the hater of good, the source of envy and wickedness, the evil devil, saw
the building of those monasteries and the salvation of many souls, did he then hold back from his wickedness?
Far from it! Instead he stirred up a kinsman of this saint, who began to curse and to swear that he would burn the monastery and kill the saint.
To confirm this evil intention, he scattered charcoal at the door of the monastery and wrote on a small board:
"This is how everyone will see this monastery within three days." And he threw the board down before the gates of the monastery.
When day broke, Saint Hilarion saw all this. He was deeply grieved and distressed over the ruin of that man's soul.
He did not mourn at all over threats and declarations against his body. Far from it! He mourned because he was merciful and loved souls. That is why he stayed all night in prayer to God.
And as he fell asleep, he saw a radiant man, who said to him:
"Do not be afraid, O Hilarion, for this very day that enemy of yours will be taught a lesson and will fall at your feet."

When day broke, at that very moment the devil struck the man to the ground. He rolled about and foamed at the mouth. His servants immediately picked him up, brought him before the saint and laid him on the ground.
But the father, who held no grudges and was full of mercy, considered that small punishment to be for the man's salvation. He rose quickly and humbly begged the Lord to heal him.
He made the sign of the precious cross over him and raised him to his feet, alive and freed from the unclean spirit.
Then the man began to confess his earlier follies with tears, and he went to his home.
He brought all his possessions to the saint for building the monastery, and he received the monastic tonsure from the saint's hands.
He became a good monk and settled in that same monastery, living a good life
in humility and obedience, counting himself lower than everyone, and serving the brothers without complaint.
In this way Saint Hilarion saved his kinsman in both lives, bodily and spiritual.
Then news of him spread throughout the whole land of Kartli.
Many people wanted and were eager to see his face with their own eyes and to hear his words, which were full of sweetness and spiritual joy.
For those who saw him, simply meeting him was of great benefit.
They gave thanks to God and brought many supplies to provide for the brothers and to serve the poor and strangers.
His soul loved stillness and hated turmoil, and he saw the people coming again and again and the disturbance this caused. For this reason he could not achieve the seclusion he longed for.
All the people, and the ruler of that land too, wanted to make him a bishop.
And when the blessed Hilarion understood this, he reasoned within himself:
"This glory of this world is a deceiver that leads to everlasting disgrace."
In this too he became like the great lawgiver Moses, by going out of Egypt again, a second time,
since he delivered many souls from slavery to that invisible Pharaoh and led them out through the sea of this world without their drowning,
and there he saw that mighty pursuer drowned along with his horsemen, and with spiritual dancing he offered a song of victory to God, the giver of victory.
When he had firmly decided in his mind to flee from vainglory and to go away to a more distant land, where he would not be known,
he chose one brother from among the brothers of the monastery, a man full of all wisdom and able to shepherd the rational sheep.
He brought him and set him before everyone, laid his holy hands on him, lifted up his eyes to heaven and said:
"I thank you, my King and my God, to whom I have been entrusted from my mother's womb until this day,
who rescued me from the snares of those who hunted me, and walked with me and struggled alongside me in all my ways,
until you willed that I should come back to this land, in which I lived and was brought up.
Thus your incomprehensible providence was pleased that through me, a poor man, this place should be built for these brothers to gather in.
Now, O good Lord, I commit these your servants into your holy hands. Guard them, O King, from the many forms and many tricks of the enemy's schemes.
Let the evil devil find no place of rest among them, but let your holy and life-giving Spirit rest upon them.
And this brother, whom your all-holy will has chosen as superior over them: bless him with every blessing with which you blessed our holy fathers.
Through the laying on of my unworthy hands, let your holy grace come upon him, so that he may guide these brothers well and increase the talent entrusted to him,
and so that you may be glorified through that good servant [?]. For yours is the glory, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen."
Then he said to that brother: "Watch well, brother, and strive for the souls of these brothers as you would for your own soul. Then the punishment of that worthless servant will not fall on you,
the one who buried his lord's talent in the ground. Instead, increase it many times over, so that, having been faithful over a little, you may be set over much and enter into the joy of your Lord."
Having said this, he turned to all the brothers and taught them at length about the salvation of their souls. He commanded them to obey the superior who had been appointed over them.
He raised his hands, committed them to the Lord and said: "Into your holy hands, Lord, I commit these brothers."
He bade them a last farewell, parted from them and went away.
But who could describe the weeping and lamenting that those brothers did, and the pitiful cries, which could have softened even stones?
Some followed behind him, and some hurried to run ahead, so that by going with him they might share [?] the road with him.
But the saint prayed and begged them to turn back, until, compelled by an oath, they fell at his holy feet and kissed them. Only then did they turn back, left orphaned by their sweet father.
Saint Hilarion took two brothers with him and went to visit the earlier monasteries that he had built before he went to Jerusalem.
He saw them and greeted all the brothers with prayer and blessing. He also instructed each of them about the salvation of their souls.
He went out from there and went to visit the monastery that had been built for his mother.
His venerable mother had departed this life. He commended all the sisters to God and blessed them. Then he went forth from there and left his own country.
By the will of God he set out for the royal city of Constantinople in the time of Michael, the faithful emperor,
who took the throne after his father Theophilus and, together with his mother Theodora, confirmed the veneration of the holy icons.
But let us return to our earlier account.
Hilarion, guided by the Holy Spirit, [?] on Mount Olympus, and he found a small church in a deserted place. He went in and stayed there.
When Saturday came, the eve of holy Sunday, a monk came from a nearby monastery to light the lamp.
He found Saint Hilarion inside with his disciples. He went to the monastery and brought him a few rusks and soaked chickpeas.
Then the saint asked the brother to bring him holy offering bread and wine for offering the bloodless sacrifice.
The brother went and the next day, holy Sunday, he brought them as the elder had asked. They celebrated the holy Liturgy.
When the brother went back to the monastery, he told all this to the abbot. As soon as the abbot heard it, he flew into a rage and said:
"Who knows whether they think rightly or hold the true faith!" At once he ordered that they be driven out with insults.
Then the steward and other brothers went and told them the abbot's order. The saint promised them that they would leave the next day.
So matters stood: the unjust order had been issued, and the saint, in keeping with the decision, was hurrying to leave the next day. Did the mercy of God perhaps approve of this?
Far from it! For that night, while the abbot was asleep, he suddenly saw a terrifying vision.
For our all-holy, all-incorrupt and most blessed Lady, the Mother of God, the ever-virgin Mary,
the helper and support of all who have become strangers and become poor for the sake of her Son's name, stood over him in a vision. In great wrath she spoke to him and said:
"O wretch, why did you want to drive out those strangers, who have come out of love for my Son and God and have left their own country,
and why did you not keep the commandment about receiving strangers and the poor, as my Lord and my Son says to that rich man?
Or do you not know that many people who speak their language are going to settle on this mountain and will be saved by God?

"And those who do not receive them are my enemies, for this people has been granted to me by my Son, unshakably, because of their orthodoxy, since they believed in the name of my Son and were baptized."
And when the abbot came to himself after the vision, he rose up trembling and began to weep from the depth of his heart, and until daybreak he did not cease from lamenting.
And as daybreak drew near, he went with bitter weeping to the church where the saint was staying with his disciples.
And when he saw him, he fell at his feet and asked forgiveness for his earlier insolence, and he implored him under oath not to leave that place, so that the holy Queen would not be angry with him.
And he told him the vision he had seen that night, and begged him to become his intercessor before the holy Mother of God.
But Saint Hilarion raised him up and said to him: "Let it be according to your will, holy father."
Then the abbot asked that they be allowed to bring him eulogia every Saturday.
And the blessed one allowed this to be done. And the abbot went back to his monastery.
Now there was a relative of his whose right foot had been injured since his youth, and he asked the abbot
to appoint him to serve the saint and to bring him the eulogia that had been arranged.
And as this brother did so and served the saint, one day, when he was bringing the eulogia as usual,
the devil, hater of good, seeing such zeal in him, made him stumble on his injured foot and caused it sharp pain.
And the brother wept bitterly from the pain. When Saint Hilarion saw him weeping, his merciful soul was grieved.
He took holy oil from the lamp of the Lord's church and anointed the painful foot, and healed both the pain and the infirmity he had suffered from. He sent him away and commanded him to tell no one.
But he told all of this to the abbot and to all the brothers, who had seen him before, and they gave thanks to God, the worker of wonders.
From then on, because of this miracle, everyone regarded him as an apostle and a shepherd.
And people came from the surrounding monasteries to see him and to receive his holy prayer. And his fame spread across all of Mount Olympus.
And they came and were filled with his teaching, and glorified God, who had given such a luminary.
Then three other Georgian brothers came to him, and the blessed Hilarion received them. One of them spoke Greek well.
And they lived in that place quietly and undisturbed, separated from every human care.
And the inhabitants of the royal city too heard of the virtues of Saint Hilarion and of his angelic way of life,
and they would come and beg him to accept from them whatever he needed. But he did not wish to do this, and said to them:
"Our helper, the holy Mother of God, feeds us, and she will not let us lack bodily food."
And when they saw his great poverty, many rose up to imitate his spotless life,

For he worked with his own hands, and from this he earned the bodily necessities for himself and for those who were with him, and he was a burden to no one. For he remembered the saying of the great apostle:
"My hands have ministered to me," and again he says: "Day and night I work with my hands, so that I may not be a burden to anyone."
And again he lays down that the idle hand should not eat. This saint acted in imitation of him.

Then he saw that the number of people coming to him was growing and that they were troubling him greatly. Because of this he could not find the life of solitude that he desired. He also wished to flee from vainglory, and he did not want
anyone to praise him, since from his youth he had cut the sinews of that devil of vain pride. This was the reason he traveled from land to land,
so that pride might never find a place in him, and the dragon of love of money might never find a nest for its wickedness.
For, as the fathers say, the [?] of the passions are born from these three: from love of glory, love of pleasure, and love of money.
For this reason this saint courageously and mightily trampled down all three of these heads of the serpent by the power of the Holy Trinity.
When Saint Hilarion saw that crowd of people coming, he spoke to his disciples as follows:
"My children, behold, I have been here five years since we came, and I have not been able to go to the City to venerate the life-giving Wood.
And now, until I come back, build a small cell out of stones, a dry-stone cell." And he taught them how it was to be built.
He took one disciple with him, named Isaac, and went to Constantinople to venerate the precious Cross and all the holy churches.
But he left his four other disciples on Olympus.
When he entered the royal city, he venerated the precious Wood that he had longed for, and he kissed with longing the holy relics, as many of them as he was able to reach. And he resolved
to go on from there to Rome to venerate the tomb of the holy and all-praised chief apostles, Peter and Paul. He set out by the will of God.
After he had traveled fourteen [?] and reached a certain city, he found a garden outside that city, and a lame man sitting at the gate of that garden.
The saint sat down with his disciple near that lame man and said to him:
"Man, get up and bring me one bunch of grapes." The man said to him:
"Look, father, this garden is before you; take whatever you wish, for I cannot get up because of my sins,
and I have been here thirteen years, ever since I became lame, and the owner of this place feeds me."
Then the saint took pity on that man. He sighed from the depth of his heart and lifted the eyes of his mind to God,
who hears those who pray in silence more than any loud cry. And he said to the man:
"Get up, brother, the Lord has commanded it. Bring me some of the fruit of that garden with your own hand."
At that very moment his feet were made straight. He stood up and went into the vineyard to bring him grapes.
But Saint Hilarion got up and went away by another road. When the man came out, he could no longer find that good healer.
And at once he went into the city, holding that cluster [?] in his hands, giving thanks to God and crying out:
"Inhabitants of this city, look at me, look at me! For I am the one who was lame before, and you saw me many times.
But now you see how I am, through the prayer of a man of God."
Then, when the people of the city saw that great wonder, those who had known the man before asked him in amazement:
"How were you healed?" And he told them the whole story of his healing, and described to them the appearance and features of the saint and of his disciple too.
Then all the people of the city quickly began to search for them in the streets, along the roads, and in every place where they might be suspected of having gone.
But by the will of God the saint was hidden from their eyes, and he went on his way wherever he wished.
God worked miracles through him all along his way, wherever he went.
And under God's guidance and with the help of the holy apostles he reached the city of Rome.
And like a deer longing for springs of water, so, burning with divine longing, he at once hurried to the church of the holy chiefs of the apostles, Peter and Paul.
He bowed down and kissed their holy tombs tearfully, with fervour of spirit, and all the holy relics of the hierarchs and martyrs that he came upon.
And he spent two years in Rome in an angelic life and in ascetic struggle, for he kept his mind fixed always on the contemplation of God.
And there too the Lord worked many miracles and healings through him,
as his disciple, the blessed Isaac, later told us in full when he returned from there after the saint's death.
Then his divine way of life became known to all the inhabitants of Rome. They were all amazed, and they came to meet him, to bow down at his holy feet, and to receive his holy prayer.
And he blessed them all and sent them away with prayer. And they gave thanks to God, who had sent this saint to their city.
And after he had spent two years in Rome in a lofty and wondrous way of life, it came into his heart, moved from on high,
to go back again to the imperial city of Constantinople. For God willed not to leave this glorious city deprived,
which has gathered within itself, and all around its whole surrounding district, multitudes of all the saints,
and willed that it should also be counted worthy to receive his relics into its wide and glorious bosom.
For this reason Saint Hilarion set out from there.
Weary, he reached the city of Thessalonica. And when he entered the city, before anything else he bowed down at the shrine of the glorious, victory-clad martyr Demetrius.
And from there he went to the praetorium of the ruler of that city and sat down in front of its gates.
And behold, by divine providence a servant woman of that ruler brought out her four-year-old son, who was half-paralysed, and laid him in the sunlight near Saint Hilarion.
Saint Hilarion said to that woman, "Woman, go and bring me water." And at once she got up to fetch the water.
Then, when that woman had gone away, Saint Hilarion rose and sighed from the depths of his heart.
He made the sign of the cross over the boy and said, "In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, I say to you, boy,
rise up alive." And immediately he was healed and stood up on his feet, completely unharmed. And he said again to the boy:
"Go, child, your mother needs you." And the boy rose up alive and went in to his mother.
But Saint Hilarion rose and went away to another place, so that those who were searching for him would not recognize him through this miracle. See now, O beloved,
what grace this holy father of ours was found worthy of, for he became like the great apostles Peter and John, who healed the lame man
who sat begging for alms before the doors of the Beautiful Gate. They granted healing by a word, and Peter also raised up Aeneas the paralytic.
And this is no less than their miracles that this blessed man performed. For when he wished to heal the first lame man,
whom he found in front of the garden, he first asked him for sweet fruit, though he himself intended to be the one giving.
And again, when he was healing this boy whom we have just mentioned, he first asked his mother for water to drink, because he intended to give her son the water of healing to drink.
And likewise, while he was staying on the mountain of Ulombo [?], he healed in this same way the lame man who brought him a eulogia (a blessed gift), and to him he gave the eulogia of healing.
And when the boy went in to his mother, as we said before, the saint went away to another place.
But the servant woman snatched up the boy and brought him to her mistress, and she asked how the boy had been healed.
And she told her the whole manner of his healing, and the description of the saint and of his disciple, and also of their language.
And immediately the lady went in and told all this to her husband, and also showed him the healed boy.
When the governor heard this, he at once ordered that the city gates be guarded quickly and that the saint be searched for.
And as they searched, they found him at the eastern gate, going out.
For a city built on a mountain cannot be hidden, nor can a burning lamp be made invisible under a bed,
for the more the saint wished to hide his deeds, the more God revealed his servant, God who glorifies those who glorify him.
When the men searching for him found the saint, they at once fell down and bowed before his holy feet and asked him for a blessing.
And the blessed man blessed them, raised them up, and went along with them.
Then, when the governor was told the saint was coming, he came out to meet him and kissed his holy feet.
But the saint blessed him, raised him up, and said to him: "May Christ, the keeper of all who love him, keep your God-loving self!"
Then the governor took the saint to his house and begged him to choose whatever place he wished and to stay there.
Then the saint, when he saw that godly and God-loving mind of the prince, allowed him to do this, and he chose a suitable and quiet place, such as befitted his holiness.
And they built a beautiful church for him in that place. And the saint instructed that they should not trouble him constantly.
And again he instructed that nothing should be brought to him except dry rusks and soaked peas.
And the prince carried out everything he had ordered.
Then word of him spread through all the land of Illyricum, and countless souls came and were edified by his teaching,
and they received his holy prayers, and so they went back to their homes.
And many of those who lived in the city were moved to emulate his godly way of life and his spotless life, and at his hands they became monks and advanced in angelic conduct and ascetic struggle.
At that time a deacon of Thessalonica went out to look over his vineyard. And the heathens seized him and carried him off to their own land.
And as he was being led away, on the road he remembered Saint Hilarion, having utterly given up hope of rescue by human means,
and he began to entreat him with hot tears and called on his holy prayers to help him.
And that very night, as he slept doubly bound with iron chains, the saint appeared to him and said to him:
"Arise, O deacon, and do not be afraid, for it is I to whom you have been praying."
And when he woke up, he found that he had been freed from his bonds. He got up at once and passed fearlessly through the whole army.
And no one knew of this event until he came to the city of Thessalonica. And he told everyone about this great miracle.
And he came to the saint and kissed his holy hands, by which he had been freed from his bonds,
and with thanksgiving he told him of the miracle that he had worked on him. The saint said to him: "My son! It was God's will that you be rescued.
For this reason he sent his angel in my likeness, since you called in faith on the name of me, a sinner, and he freed you from bitter captivity.
So give thanks to God, the worker of miracles." And the deacon went home a free man and glorified God.
And Saint Hilarion remained for some time in the city of Thessalonica, with ascetic struggle beyond the strength of nature,
for he forgot all the struggles of his youth mentioned above, and, like one newly entering the stadium of ascetic struggle, he was more fervent in his desire than before,
for, in the words of the Apostle, he did not remember at all the labors that were past and was eager to reach forward to those that lay ahead.
For this reason God glorified him with signs and healings while he was still in this life,
for some he healed of bodily illnesses, and others he freed from spiritual passions and afflictions, and so he brought countless souls to God.
And when the time came for his death, for his departure from here and his going to God alone,
which he had longed for, and for whose name he had struggled from his early youth, he was told of it by God.
And the appearance of his face changed and he became joyful in spirit, like a good laborer going to gather the fruit of his virtues, as David says:
"They came with joy, bringing their sheaves."
or like a victorious soldier who has destroyed the enemy and is going to his king,
or like a skilful ship's captain who brings many souls safely across, without sinking, amid the waves of the sea of this world, and offers them to God.
Then he called the governor and said to him: "O governor, you have done well in taking in this poor man and stranger."
May the Lord give you the reward of love, who in his strangeness has made us, who were strangers, one with God the Father [?].
"From now on, be eager to take in the poor and monks, and above all strangers.
Guard yourself against robbing the poor, and against every unjust and unrighteous deed,
so that the mercy of God may protect you in this life and make you a sharer forever in the kingdom with the saints.
For behold, I am now going the way of my fathers, and the time of my departure has come."
Then the governor began to weep, and he kissed his holy hands and his face.
And the saint lifted up his hands to God, prayed over him, blessed him, and sent him away to his home.
And when Saturday came, the saint called his disciples and said to them:
"My children, know that my time has come, and behold, I must now leave the earthly dwelling of my flesh, as the apostle Peter says.
From now on look to yourselves and take good care for the life of your souls until your very last breath. Know wisely that our enemy,
like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom among us he may devour; but may the invincible right hand of God deliver us from his mouth.
Now, my children, guard yourselves and love one another, and may the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding,
keep you under the shelter of his glory, and may his grace and mercy be with your spirit. Amen."
And he blessed them and taught them much about the life of their souls.
After this he received the holy mysteries of Christ God, lifted up his hands, offered thanks, and gave up his soul to the holy angels without distress or pain.
Then they informed the governor, and he came with the archbishop and all the people, with a multitude of priests and deacons, to honour that holy body.

And when the inhabitants of the city also learned of it, at once people of every age came, young men and old, together with children and women, with a multitude of candles and incense, with psalms and hymns.
Every one of them was eager to touch his holy body, or to obtain some piece of his clothing as a blessing.
And the governor ordered a marble coffin to be brought, so that they might lay the holy body to rest in it.
And when his burial was about to take place, two men possessed by demons suddenly came and said:
"Hilarion the Georgian, why are you driving us out of our dwellings?" And as soon as they came near his holy body, they were healed.
And when all the people saw this great and glorious wonder, they all gave thanks to God.
Then they anointed his holy body with myrrh, and only with difficulty did they lay it in the coffin, because of the crush of the people.
For a multitude of priests and deacons, monks and laypeople had come, as we said before, to honour his holy body.
And on that day God worked many miracles and healings through him in the city of Thessalonica. For while this saint was in the flesh,
he did not wish to receive glory from people; but God, who glorifies those who glorify him, glorified him after his death.
Our holy father Hilarion died on the 19th of the month of November, on a Saturday, at the fifth hour of the day,
in the reign of Basil the Macedonian, who received the kingship after Michael.
This Michael was the one who confirmed the veneration of the holy icons, as we said above, and he was also called "the Drunkard."
But let us return to our earlier account. This saint passed away at the age of fifty-three, in the city of Thessalonica.
And the inhabitants of the city celebrated his commemoration year by year at the time recorded above, when he passed away.
And many miracles and healings took place at his tomb.
The son of the city's ruler fell ill, and his private parts and his belly swelled up. The physicians gave up hope for him, until he came close to death.
Then his parents took him up and laid him before the saint's sarcophagus.
And that night Saint Hilarion appeared and spoke thus to the one who had been given up for lost:
"O Procopius" (for that was the youth's name), "believe me: unless you promise me that you will not live a dissolute life, you will not be healed of that illness."
And he promised on oath to do this. Then the saint laid his hand on his belly and said to him:
"In the name of Jesus Christ, be well," and he made the sign of the cross over him. And he was healed at once.
And when he woke up, he glorified God and the saint, for no affliction at all remained in him.
And he kissed the saint's holy sarcophagus and told all the people about this great and glorious wonder. And those who heard it glorified God.
This saint's disciples gave one of the saint's hair garments to a poor widow.
She received it from them as worth more than any treasure or precious jewels, with hope and great faith. And any sick person she covered with it found relief.
And people told one another about these wonders and gave thanks to God, to whom be glory, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and for ever and ever. Amen.
At that time, as the signs and wonders of our blessed father Hilarion became widely known, news of them reached the God-serving emperor Basil from every side as well:
wonders that were taking place day after day in the city of Thessalonica. For the ruler of the city and the archbishop had also written him a letter,
It told of the saint's death and of the miracles of healing that were taking place before his holy tomb.
When the emperor had read the letter, he summoned all the officials of the palace and told them what the letter sent from Thessalonica was about. When they heard it, they gave thanks to God.
In those same days the God-serving emperor wished to gather all the abbots of Mount Olympus to the imperial city about a certain matter that needed their attention.
One day they all came to the palace. When they came before him, the emperor rejoiced in spirit with them at seeing them.
They began to speak spiritual words before the emperor.
Then the emperor began to tell them about the deeds and miracles of this saint, and how the governor of the city and the archbishop had written to him about them from Thessalonica.
Now the abbot from Olympus heard this. He was the one who had first received holy Hilarion, and it was his sister's son, a lame man, who had been healed.
At once he began to tell the emperor about the deeds of holy Hilarion and the wonders he had worked in his monastery.
He also told him of the vision of the all-holy Mother of God. The emperor asked: "Are any of his disciples still on that mountain?"
He answered: "Yes, holy emperor. Three of his disciples are there, old men, worthy and pleasing to God."
Then the God-serving emperor ordered that his disciples be brought to the palace with all speed on an imperial dromon, with great honour fitting their worth.
When the holy fathers reached the imperial city and the emperor was told, he at once ordered them to be brought before him.
When they came in, the emperor rejoiced with great joy at the sight of their angelic appearance, for the holy elders were advanced in days and venerable in age.
The beauty of their outward appearance clearly showed the inner radiance of their souls, and their contrite and humble speech revealed the meekness and calm of their minds.
The emperor begged them to pray for him and for his whole empire. The blessed men raised their hands and blessed the emperor together with his whole empire.
Then the emperor said: "Truly, here are servants of God and intercessors for my soul before God! Glory to you,
O Christ the King, who have made me, this unworthy emperor, worthy to see the worthy ones who are pleasing to your kingship."
[?] imperial gifts, he sent them to the holy Patriarch Ignatius. Because of his holiness and worth, Ignatius was at that time patriarch over this imperial city.
He sent him this message: "See these men who are equal to the angels, and receive their prayer. I have seen them, and I rejoiced greatly at the very sight of them.
For looking upon their venerable appearance was better than conversing with others.
And their delightful and spiritual words also showed the innocence and simplicity of their minds."
When the patriarch saw the holy fathers, he greeted them warmly with brotherly love. He rejoiced greatly, blessed them, and received their prayer.
The patriarch spoke with those blessed men, his bishops being with him, in spiritual words, and he came to know their worthiness and their true faith.
And he said to the bishops: "Truly these are spiritual treasures, which no thief can come near;
seeing them today has granted me great grace." And he sent word to the king, saying:
"O God-loving king, great good has come to me today through you, by my seeing these holy fathers. Truly these are servants of the Lord and intercessors for our souls.
Through their prayer may your God-crowned reign be firm and undisturbed forever. Amen."
Then the God-serving and God-loving king summoned those holy men and said to them:
"O honored fathers, let your worthiness choose a monastery, wherever you wish, for yourselves and for your people." But they answered:
"O king, this is not possible for us: that we, men who are foreigners, should take over what others have built and drive out those who built it.
In that way we would bring a curse upon your reign instead of a prayer. Let us not do so, O king, let us not do so.
Instead, if you are willing, let us go out to a deserted place and look for a quiet spot where it would be fitting to build a monastery.
And if God wills it, build us a church there as a house of prayer for your God-serving majesty."
When the God-serving king heard this, he was filled with joy and said to them:
"Good, good, honorable fathers. Go, then, and search everywhere, and tell me which place pleases your holiness, and I will do everything as you command."
And he sent them with a man of the royal court to look wherever they wished.
They left the palace and went to a wooded and deserted place. In a valley they found springs, and the ground was level and beautiful. They rejoiced greatly and reported it to the God-serving king.
When he heard, he came to that place with his people. The king himself carried stones, and so did all the people with him.
They began to build the church and the monastery, and in seven months they completed all the work on the monastery.

Then the king came with the patriarch and held the dedication, and they placed relics of the holy apostles there on the 9th of October. The king donated vessels of gold and silver, villages and estates, and a metochion (dependent house) in the city.
He also gave them the forests that surrounded that place, and he generously provided everything needed, as is fitting for a monastery.

The king built a small cell for himself and placed in it a bed for himself with its bedding. He set up bookstands and put books on them, the Gospel and the Apostle (the Epistles of Paul), and he said:
"Let this be my dwelling near these worthy fathers, so that through their prayers God may be pleased to deliver me from the retribution for my sins."
He named that place the Monastery of the Georgians; its original name had been Romana.
Then the king said to those worthy fathers: "Holy fathers! Ask for whatever you need from my kingdom." And they said to him:
"We ask of you, O God-loving king, that you remove all injustice from your realm, so that you do not make the Lord angry with you, and so that your kindness toward us does not come to nothing."
When the king heard this, he rejoiced at these words, and his faith in them grew greater.
He loved them more than all the people of that time. He brought his two sons, Leo and Alexander, and said to them:
"Pray for them, holy fathers, and teach them letters in your language, so that they may be children of your prayer."
After this the king and the patriarch went away to the city.
When the God-loving king had done all this well, God was pleased with his good deed and revealed it in a vision to the great recluse, the ascetic Euthymius,
who at that time was a holy and God-clothed man. He knew all the thoughts of the king's heart.
He wrote to the king as follows: "I saw in a vision a terrible smoke of fire, and I heard a voice that said:
'These are the sins of King Basil.' And I said: 'Who is able to quench this?'
And again I heard a voice: 'Tears and good deeds.'
At once radiant men took your good deeds and threw them into the fire, and with great labour they began to quench it.
Then those who were over that furnace heard a voice: 'Bring the receiving of strangers too!'
And they brought something small, like a grain of wheat, and white as snow, and threw it into it.
Only then did the smoke and the fire begin to vanish completely. Now therefore, O king, make haste to receive strangers and the poor, and above all monks."
When the king had read the letter of that great recluse, he first gave thanks to the merciful God, and then he summoned the eparch of Thessalonica,
who had been appointed over the imperial taxes, and who had earlier written about the death of Saint Hilarion and the account of his miracles.
He gave him the highest honour and sent him to Thessalonica, so that he might bring the relics of the blessed father Hilarion with great honour.

For this was fitting for this saint, who from his very childhood had of his own will offered his soul and body, spotless and purified, to his Creator without blemish, so that he should likewise be doubly honoured in soul and in body.
For when the invisible soul of the saint left the dwelling of his holy body,
the invisible King of all at once took it up into the invisible city of the firstborn, the heavenly Jerusalem, and settled it there in glory.
And again, a little later, when the glories of the signs of his wonders had spread abroad,
the earthly and visible king, into this new Jerusalem and visible imperial city, his visible relics
decided to bring up with glory, for the city and the people to see, as a hope and an intercessor for the stability of his own reign, and as a protector of the city and the people.
And so, divided in two, he was honoured twice over, as a reward for his virtues and struggles.
But let us return to our earlier account. The God-serving King Basil wrote a letter of the following kind to Thessalonica, as we said before:
"Our Majesty commands the Thessalonians to send, with great haste and imperial glory, the relics of Saint Hilarion the Georgian,
without any excuse or resistance, and farewell!" And he also wrote to the saint with his own hand, as follows:
"Basil the emperor, sinful servant of the King of heaven: I beseech you, holy father Hilarion, come up to the imperial city. Although I was not found worthy to see you face to face,
make me worthy now to kiss your holy relics. Let this imperial city rejoice at their arrival, and may your grace be with us. Amen."
When the envoys arrived, they read out the imperial command before all the people.
As soon as the people understood what the letter meant, a riot and an uproar broke out in the city.
They all plotted together to stone the emperor's men.
The governor of the city managed to calm the people's uprising only with difficulty. And they promised the envoys that they would not do this.
Then the proconsul rose and went out to the surrounding villages. He ordered the envoys to take up the saint's relics by night, without the people knowing.
They did so and placed the relics in a small casket. They sealed up the sarcophagus in which the holy relics had lain, just as it had been, and left without anyone knowing.
At daybreak the inhabitants of the city learned all of this. They began to grieve and lament at being separated from the saint.
Some embraced the empty sarcophagus. Others gazed out toward the sea, as though they thought he had not yet sailed away from there.
Others reproached him as if he were alive, and complained that he had abandoned the city where he had passed away and gone to God.
So, filled with inconsolable grief, they fled to the sarcophagus of his holy relics. They entrusted their whole life to it, and from it they received consolation.
When the saint's relics reached the God-guarded imperial city, this was made known to the God-serving and faithful emperor.
He then ordered the patriarch, together with the bishops, priests and deacons, all the nobles and the people of the city, to come out all together to meet the saint.

The emperor went out with the patriarch and all the people as far as the seashore, with hymns and litanies, a multitude of candles and the fragrance of incense. And they brought him to the imperial palace.
The emperor laid him to rest in the chapel of his palace and considered in his mind where he should build a shrine for the saint's relics.
On the third night after the saint had been brought there, the emperor was sleeping on his bed.
And behold, a wondrous fragrance spread through the whole palace.
The emperor woke from sleep at once and smelled an indescribable fragrance. He wondered to himself what it was, or which incense it came from.
Since he could not work it out, he asked the eunuchs who were sleeping around him: "What is this fragrance?"
They answered: "We swear by your majesty, we have never known such a fragrance."
The whole palace came to know of it, and each person asked his companion: "What kind of fragrance is this?"
And they could not recognize [him]. But by God's providence, when the king had fallen asleep again, Saint Hilarion suddenly appeared to him, clothed in a priestly vestment, and said to him:
"You did well to receive me, O king, this stranger and poor man.
"But this fragrance that you smelled, I did not gain it in cities but in deserts."
"Now if you wish to have the grace in full, take me away to a desert place."
When the king woke up, he rose at once and gave thanks to the saint, who had revealed his will to him.
He told all of this to those who were in the palace. They all rose and sang before the saint's reliquary until dawn.
When dawn came, the king summoned the patriarch and all the officials of the palace. He told them about the fragrance and the saint's vision, and he spoke to them thus:
"Know that the saint wishes to be in the desert." And he decided to move him to the monastery that he had built for the saint's disciples.
At once he held a litany, and he ordered the saint's relics to be taken up. He boarded the royal boats (agraria) and set out for the monastery mentioned above.
First he went into the church of the Archangel Michael at Sosthenion, and he also brought the saint's relics inside.
When he had prayed before that glorious commander of the heavenly hosts, he came out from there, mounted the royal chariots, and went to Romana,
which he himself had built for the disciples of this saint, as we said earlier.
When he entered the church, he first venerated the relics of the holy apostles.
Then he held a litany and prayers, and on the 7th of December he laid the relics of Saint Hilarion to rest in that same small reliquary.
When the saint's disciples saw their teacher's relics, they were like children who love their father and have long yearned for him;
in tears they began to kiss the relics. With raised hands they thanked God, who brings all good things to completion, and then they blessed the God-loving king.
The king donated twelve drahkans (silver coins) a month to that church,

so that six lamps would burn at all times over the relics of the holy apostles and three lamps over the relics of Saint Hilarion, and so that two royal loaves would be given from the palace every day,
and so that two litras of gold would be given from the palace for the monks' clothing in the month of December, on the 7th. And he named the monastery after himself.
Then the God-serving king and the patriarch venerated and kissed the saint's relics. They returned to the city and gave thanks to God.
Basil, protoasekretis, philosopher and venerable monk, wrote down this life of the saint as he learned it from the saint's disciples, men who were truthful and did not lie.
But let us thank God for all this, the worker of wonders. To him belongs the glory, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, now and for all ages, forever and ever. Amen.
